take: US crude imports from Venezuela averaged 701,000 b/d in July, the highest since 2017 before easing to 655,000 b/d in August, which matters because heavy sour replacement barrels are loosening the Atlantic Basin crude slate just as US refiners run above 95% utilisation and push yields towards middle distillates on strong distillate and jet margins. On the freight side, Volare’s $210m Trafigura-linked VLCC newbuilding and Torm’s eight-ship LR2 programme at Yangzijiang point to continued tanker capacity expansion, whilst Monjasa’s five-tanker product carrier swoop from Bernhard Schulte signals bunker suppliers positioning for marine fuels volumes rather than any near-term tightening in tonne-miles. The inventory angle is the refinery yield shift itself: with global crude runs having fallen 4.8 million b/d, or 6%, in 2Q26 before a modest recovery, the marginal barrel is being pulled towards distillate, so watch gasoil and jet cracks rather than gasoline for the cleaner signal. The cross-market link sits in the middle distillate complex versus bunker: high distillate margins incentivise maximum middle-distillate yield, which competes with VLSFO availability for the bunker pool, so a widening gasoil–HSFO spread would squeeze scrubber economics and support higher-sulphur bunker demand. For the next 24 hours, watch the weekly EIA petroleum status report for confirmation that utilisation stays above 95% and distillate stocks draw, plus any crude reaction to the Nvidia board headlines dragging Nasdaq-100 futures lower, which could feed through risk sentiment into flat price.
